topic.title: Data Structures in C: linked lists, stacks, queues
topic.description: The three structures every interview asks about, built from scratch in C: a node, a head pointer, and the links between them — plus the stack (LIFO) and the queue (FIFO) that sit on top of the same idea.

curriculum.summary: A linked list, a stack and a queue are one idea in three costumes: a structure that owns its own memory and decides where the next thing goes. In C that means a pointer inside a struct. This topic starts from that node and builds the whole family up — malloc, the head pointer, insert at the front, insert at a position, delete (two jobs, not one), traverse, reverse, then the stack (LIFO) and the queue (FIFO) on both an array and a list. Every video is measured: the numbers next to each one are the real views, likes, length and channel, read off the watch page, not a guess. The lowest reach of any video in this pack is 535,687 views; the one that was rejected when this topic was written had 327.

rules.commentPolicy: Every non-obvious line needs a WHY comment, not a WHAT comment. A comment that restates the code is deleted. A comment that states the reason is kept. In this topic that means a comment on every malloc, every link you change, and every index you move.
rules.notePolicy: Write three lines maximum: what you learned, what broke, what is next. If it needs more than 220 characters per line, it is not understood yet.

explanation.h: 1. Why this topic starts with pointers
explanation.md:
A linked list, a stack and a queue are the same idea wearing different clothes: **a structure that owns its own memory and decides where the next thing goes.** In C, "decides where the next thing goes" means *a pointer inside a struct*. If pointers are still shaky, this topic will be noise. So watch the pointer course first, and if `malloc` still feels like magic, watch its dynamic memory chapter before you write anything.

One C fact to hold onto for the whole topic: **C has no garbage collector.** Every byte you ask for with `malloc`, you give back with `free`, by hand. That single fact explains most of the bugs in this topic.

explanation.h: 2. What a data structure actually is
explanation.md:
A **data structure** is a way of storing and organising data so that it can be used efficiently. Every structure has two halves:

- The **abstract data type (ADT)** — what you are allowed to do. Push, pop, enqueue, dequeue. No mention of arrays, pointers or memory.
- The **implementation** — how it is actually done in your language.

The same ADT has several possible implementations. "A stack" could be an array with an index, or a linked list. "A list" could be an array, a linked list, or a growable array. The ADT is the contract; the implementation is your choice. When someone asks "what is a stack?", the good answer starts with the contract, not the code.

explanation.h: 3. The node: a struct that points at itself
4. `head`: the only identity a list has
explanation.md:
```c
struct Node *head = NULL;
```

`head` is **a pointer variable**, not a node. It holds the address of the first node, and that address is the *entire* identity of the list. If you lose it, the list is gone — no matter how many nodes are still allocated.

`NULL` means "points to nothing", and it is how you spell the end of a list. Every list operation ends the same way: keep a pointer to the current node, follow `next`, and stop when the pointer is `NULL`.

Careful with the vocabulary: `head` is the *pointer*, the *head node* is the node it points at. Mixing the two up is how you end up writing `head->next` when you meant `head->next->next`.

explanation.h: 5. Building a list — malloc, fill, link
explanation.md:
Every insert into a linked list is the same three steps, no matter where the node goes:

```c
temp = malloc(sizeof(struct Node)); /* 1. ask for the memory */
temp->data = value;                 /* 2. fill in the value  */
temp->next = NULL;                  /* 3. set the link       */
```

Step 3 comes **before** you link the node into the chain, and it is not optional. A node whose `next` still holds garbage will be followed into random memory the first time somebody walks the list. Set it to `NULL` — it is the last node for now — and re-point it when you attach it.

`malloc` returns a `void *`, so it must be cast: `temp = (struct Node *)malloc(sizeof(struct Node));`. `malloc` can also return `NULL` if the machine is out of memory. At this size you can ignore that check, but know the check exists.

explanation.h: 6. Insert at the front — and why the order of two lines matters
explanation.md:
```c
temp->next = head;  /* the new node points at the old head */
head = temp;        /* the new node becomes the head       */
```

**Swap those two lines and the list is destroyed.** If `head = temp` comes first, `head` no longer knows where the old first node is; then `temp->next = head` points the new node at *itself*, and the rest of the list is orphaned — still allocated, but unreachable and leaked forever.

This is the classic pointer bug of the whole topic, and it is not a C problem. It is an ordering problem.

Because both operations are pointer assignments, inserting at the front is **O(1)** — constant time, however long the list is. That is the payoff of the linked list over an array, where inserting at the front means shifting every element along.

explanation.h: 7. Insert at a position — you need the node *before* it
explanation.md:
To insert at position `n` you need the node at position `n-1`, because that is the node whose link has to be cut:

```c
fresh->next = walk->next;  /* the new node takes the next node's place */
walk->next = fresh;        /* and the node before it now points here   */
```

Same ordering trap: build the new link **before** you break the old one. If you write `walk->next = fresh;` first, then `walk->next` no longer tells you where the rest of the list is, and `fresh->next = walk->next` would point the new node at itself.

Two special cases to write down as comments: position 1 (the new node becomes the head) and a position past the end (the new node is appended).

explanation.h: 8. Delete a node — two jobs, and people forget the second
explanation.md:
Deleting is **two** jobs, not one:

1. **Fix the links** so that nothing points at the dead node.
2. **Free the memory** with `free(dead)`.

Do only the first and you get a working program that leaks. Do only the second and you get a dangling pointer: the list still points at memory that has been handed back to the system, so the next traversal reads whatever happens to be there now. That is the bug that crashes a program tomorrow, not today.

```c
walk->next = dead->next;  /* 1. cut it out of the chain */
free(dead);                /* 2. give the memory back  */
```

Deleting the head is its own case, because `head` itself has to move first: `head = head->next;` and then `free(dead)`.

explanation.h: 10. Reverse the list — save `next` before you overwrite it
explanation.md:
Reversing is not "print the values backwards". The data stays exactly where it is; **only the links change.** Every node's `next` pointer is turned around to point back at the node you came from.

That is the hard part: once you overwrite `current->next`, the only way forward is gone. So save it first.

```c
struct Node *ahead = current->next; /* save the way forward      */
current->next = previous;           /* turn the link around      */
previous = current;                 /* remember where we came from */
current = ahead;                    /* carry on from where we were */
```

Three pointers, one pass: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. When the loop ends, `previous` points at the old last node — which is the new head.

This is the most asked linked-list question in interviews, and it is four lines. The difficulty was never the code; it was knowing which line had to come first.

explanation.h: 11. Stack: LIFO and its four operations
explanation.md:
A **stack** is a list with one restriction: insertion and deletion happen at the **same end**, called the **top**. That makes it **LIFO** — last in, first out.

The contract (the ADT) is four operations:

| Operation | What it does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `push(x)` | put `x` on top | O(1) |
| `pop()` | take the top value off and return it | O(1) |
| `top()` / `peek()` | look at the top without removing it | O(1) |
| `isEmpty()` | is there anything in it? | O(1) |

A real stack is a pile of plates: you take the top one, and you put the new one on top. That is the whole idea.

Where you meet stacks every day: **function calls**. The call stack is what makes recursion work — each call pushes a frame, each return pops one. "Last in first out" is not an academic detail.

explanation.h: 12. Stack on an array and on a list
13. Queue: FIFO, front and rear, and the circular array
explanation.md:
A **queue** is a list with the opposite restriction: insertion at one end (**rear**), removal at the other (**front**). That makes it **FIFO** — first in, first out.

| Operation | What it does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `enqueue(x)` | put `x` at the rear | O(1) |
| `dequeue()` | take the front value off and return it | O(1) |
| `front()` | look at the front without removing it | O(1) |
| `isEmpty()` | is there anything in it? | O(1) |

A real queue is the line at a shop: the person who arrived first is served first.

**On an array** you need two indices, `front` and `rear`. Here is the problem: if dequeueing only does `front = front + 1`, the slots at the start of the array are dead forever, and a long-running queue runs out of array even while it holds one element. The fix is the **circular array** — when an index runs past the end, it wraps to the start.

```c
rear  = (rear  + 1) % SIZE;
front = (front + 1) % SIZE;
```

**On a linked list** you need **two** pointers, `front` and `rear`, not just `head`. With only a head pointer, enqueueing at the back means walking the whole list (O(n)). Keeping a rear pointer makes both ends O(1).

That extra pointer is the whole lesson of the queue: when a structure has two active ends, you keep a pointer to each.

- [ ] Does every `malloc` have a matching `free` on every path out of the program?
- [ ] Does a node's `next` get set to `NULL` before the node is linked into a chain?
- [ ] Did you build the new link **before** you broke the old one?
- [ ] Did you walk the list with a separate cursor, so `head` is still intact afterwards?
- [ ] Did you test the end of the list with `NULL`, and never compare a pointer with a number?
- [ ] On a stack: is `top` initialised to `-1`, and do you check for overflow?
- [ ] On a queue: do you wrap the indices with `% SIZE`?

If any answer is "no", the comment in your code should say which one you are fixing, and why.

tasks.title: One list, one node per value
tasks.prompt: Read an integer N (1 to 100), then N integers. Build a singly linked list that holds the N values in the order you read them. Print every value on its own line, in list order.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY you set the new node's next pointer to NULL before you link it into the list.
hints: A node is a struct with a value and a pointer to the next node. Where does the struct go? On the heap.
malloc(sizeof(struct Node)) gives you a node-sized block of memory; malloc(sizeof(int)) would give you four bytes and nothing to point at.
Keep one pointer to the head of the list, and one cursor you use to walk it.

tasks.title: Push to the front
tasks.prompt: Read an integer N (1 to 100), then N integers. Insert each value at the FRONT of a singly linked list, so the list ends up holding the values in the reverse of the order you read them. Print every value on its own line.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY the line that points the new node at the old head has to come before the line that moves the head.
hints: Two lines: one makes the new node point at the old head, the other makes the new node the head.
Try swapping those two lines and see what the list prints afterwards.
Both operations are pointer assignments, so inserting at the front costs the same however long the list is.

tasks.title: Insert at a position
tasks.prompt: Read an integer N (1 to 100), then N integers, then a position P (1-based) and a value V. Insert V into the list so that it becomes the P-th element. Print every value on its own line.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY you set the new node's next pointer before you change the link of the node before it.
hints: To insert at position P you need the node at position P-1 — that is the node whose link you have to re-point.
Build the new link first, then break the old one. If you do it the other way round you lose the way to the rest of the list.
Position 1 and a position past the end are both special cases. Write them down as comments.

tasks.title: Delete at a position
tasks.prompt: Read an integer N (1 to 100), then N integers, then a position P (1-based). Delete the P-th node from the list and give its memory back. Print the values that are left, one per line. If P is outside the list, print the list unchanged.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY deleting a node is two jobs, and what breaks if you only do one of them.
hints: Deleting is not one line. Fix the links, and then free the node.
Deleting the first node is a separate case, because the head pointer itself has to move.
C does not collect garbage. If you do not call free, the memory is gone for good.

tasks.title: Reverse the list
tasks.prompt: Read an integer N (1 to 100), then N integers. Build a singly linked list, then reverse it by changing the links — do not copy the values into an array and print them backwards. Print every value on its own line.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY you save the next pointer before you overwrite it with the previous one.
hints: Reversing does not move any data. Only the next pointers change.
You need three pointers: the current node, the node you came from, and the node you are going to.
The last node you visit becomes the new head.

tasks.title: Sum of the values
tasks.prompt: Read an integer N (1 to 100), then N integers. Build a singly linked list and print the sum of the values it holds.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY you use long long for the sum instead of int.
hints: A list has no index, so you have to walk it with a cursor and add each value as you go.
A sum of many int values can be bigger than an int can hold.
Use a separate cursor for walking. Do not walk with head, or the list loses its identity.

tasks.title: A stack: push, pop, peek
tasks.prompt: Read an integer N (2 to 100), then N integers. Push them onto a stack of at most 100 values — an array plus a top index, where top starts at -1 to mean the stack is empty. Then pop one value off and print it. Then print the value that is now on top of the stack, without removing it. Print each on its own line.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY top starts at -1 and why push increments it before it writes.
hints: The stack is an int array of 100 and one index. That is the whole implementation.
Push: move the top up one, then write the value there. Pop: take the value, then move the top down one.
Peek reads the top without moving it, so the same value can be read twice.

tasks.title: A queue: fill it, then drain it
tasks.prompt: Read an integer N (1 to 4), then N integers, then one more value V. Put the N values into a queue that holds at most 4 values — an array with a front index and a rear index, where the indices wrap back to 0 when they run past the end of the array. Then take one value out of the queue and print it. Then put V into the queue. Then take everything that is left out, one per line, and print it.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY the front and rear indices wrap back to 0 instead of just counting up.
hints: A queue is an array plus two indices: front is where the next value comes out, rear is where the last value went in.
If the indices only counted up, the slots at the start of the array would be dead forever and a long queue would run out of array.
Wrapping is just the modulo: next = (index + 1) % SIZE.

written.q: Why is `malloc` needed for a linked list when an array of the same size would be simpler?
written.a: Because a linked list grows one node at a time, so the size is not known when the program starts, and each node only needs memory for itself rather than one contiguous block. malloc hands out memory at run time, so the list can grow.
written.partial: Says the size is not known in advance and that malloc allocates at run time.

written.q: Why must a new node's `next` be set to NULL before it is linked into the list?
written.a: Because until it is linked it still holds whatever was in that memory, and a walk of the list that follows an uninitialised next pointer goes into random memory. Setting it to NULL first means it is the end of the list until the real link is written.
written.partial: Says an uninitialised next pointer sends the walk somewhere random.

written.q: In `temp->next = head; head = temp;`, what breaks if you swap the two lines?
written.a: The list is destroyed. If head is moved first, head no longer knows where the old first node is, so temp->next = head points the new node at itself and the rest of the list is orphaned and leaked. The new link has to be built before the old one is broken.
written.partial: Says the order matters and that the new link must be built first.

written.q: Why is deleting a node two jobs, and what breaks if you only do one of them?
written.a: Deleting is fixing the links so nothing points at the dead node, and then freeing the memory. Skip the free and the program leaks. Skip the link fix and you leave a dangling pointer, so the next traversal reads memory that has been handed back.
written.partial: Says deleting needs both free and fixing the links, and names the leak or the dangling pointer.

written.q: A stack is O(1) for push and pop. What has to be true for a linked-list stack to be O(1)?
written.a: The push and the pop have to happen at the same end, and that end has to be the head, because reaching the tail of a linked list is O(n). Inserting and deleting at the head are both constant time.
written.partial: Says push and pop must be at the head, or that the tail costs O(n).

written.q: Why does a queue implemented on an array need to wrap its indices back to zero?
written.a: Because if the front index only counted up, the slots it leaves behind at the start of the array could never be used again, and a long-running queue would run out of array while holding only a few values. Wrapping the index with modulo reuses those slots.
written.partial: Says the front index must wrap so the old slots get used again.
